newsitem.title: USA: U.S. denies commitment to pro-Kurd policy in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denies commitment to pro-Kurd policy in Iraq.

text.p: The Clinton administration said Wednesday it was not committed to keeping President Saddam Hussein from restoring control over the ethnic "safe haven" in northern Iraq set up after the 1991 war in the Gulf.

In testimony before the House International Relations Committee, the State Department's top policy-maker on Iraq faulted rival Kurdish factions for having given Saddam the opportunity to interfere in their decades-old disputes.

"We have no commitment to protect them against their own bad judgment if one party invites Saddam Hussein in" to help it against the other, Robert Pelletreau, assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs, said.

Pressed by Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana, the panel's ranking Democrat, on whether the administration was committed to defending a Kurdish zone in the north from feared Iraqi repression, Pelletreau replied, "That has not been the policy of this administration."

Pelletreau acknowledged that the administration of George Bush, Clinton's predecessor, "may have" declared its intention to protect the Kurds in an enclave north of the 39th parallel. The area is one of two broad belts over Iraq where U.S. and allied warplanes patrol to keep Iraqi aircraft from making overflights.
Asked whether the United States should expect one challenge per year from Saddam, as has been roughly the case since the end of the war, Pelletreau replied, "I think that's a realistic possibility."

Earlier this month, the United States fired 44 cruise missiles at Iraqi military targets and enlarged the no-fly zone in southern Iraq after Saddam sent troops into the quasi-autonomous Kurdish zone to back one Kurdish faction against another, which had allied itself with Iran.
Pelletreau said the United States had never given any thought to "protecting the Kurds against themselves ... when their internal rivalries spill over."
"Our policy objective on Iraq is constant: to deter the threat the Iraqi regime poses to the peace and security of a region of vital national interest to the United States," he said.

He described the situation in the north as "fluid" after the Iraqi-assisted capture of Arbil Aug. 31 by the Kurdish Democratic Party of Nashirwan Barzani, the event that triggered the U.S. cruise missile strike.
Pelletreau, who met Barzani in Ankara a week ago, quoted the Kurdish leader as saying his party was in the process of consolidating its control over the north without Iraq's aid.

He said he had invited Barzani to send a KDP delegation to the United States. Although Barzani himself did not plan to visit, a team will come at a date to be fixed, Pelletreau said. He said the United States would also maintain contacts with the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, which had reached out to Iran.

The United States, France and Britain offered protection to Kurds in the north after the U.N. Security Council passed Resolution 688, calling on Iraq not to repress its minorities, such as the Kurds in the north and the Shi'ite Moslems in the south.

The hearing began on a highly partisan note, with panel chairman Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, deploring what he called a "failure of U.S. leadership" that had left the administration's policy of simultaneously containing Iraq and Iran "on the ropes."

Tom Lantos, a California Democrat, shot back at Gilman that he was appalled at efforts to turn the International Relations Committee into a "wholly owned subsidiary of the Republican National Committee" and an arm of Bob Dole's campaign to unseat Clinton.
